name: Dominican Republic
summary: No official Dominican page describing the entry of a casket could be found. In practice the receiving Dominican funeral home and the Dominican consulate in the country of departure state the requirements; confirm with them before booking.
documents: Death certificate from the country of death (Spanish translation likely required; confirm with the Dominican consulate)
Embalming certificate
Removal or transit permit from the country of departure
Passport or identity document of the deceased
Name of the receiving Dominican funeral home
coffin: Not published officially. A hermetically sealed coffin is the usual international standard for air transport; confirm with the Dominican consulate and the airline.
embalming: No Dominican entry rule was found. Embalming is normally required by the departure country and by carriers; the UK government lists an embalming certificate among the documents for repatriation out of the Dominican Republic.
consular: Not published officially; the Dominican consulate in the country of departure is the likely point of contact for any legalisation or authorisation. Confirm with the consulate.
arrival: Not published officially. The receiving Dominican funeral home normally handles customs and health clearance at the airport. Confirm burial or cremation formalities with the funeral home.
private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; the documents travel with the coffin and are presented to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. The coffin (typically about 2.2 m long, 70-100 kg once zinc-lined) must physically fit the aircraft's cargo door or a cabin configured for it, which rules out many light and midsize jets. Land at an international airport with customs and health officers (for example Santo Domingo Las Americas or Punta Cana) and have the receiving funeral home meet the aircraft. No specific rule for private flights carrying remains was found.
private_jet_note: Confirm entry documents with the Dominican consulate before take-off.
export: To send a body out of the Dominican Republic, the death is registered at the local Civil Registry office (Oficialia del Registro Civil), usually within about 3 working days. All foreign nationals who die in the country undergo a post-mortem at the Pathology Institute in Santo Domingo or Santiago. The UK government lists the documents for repatriation as the civil registry death certificate, an embalming certificate and a certificate giving permission to transfer the remains. Dominican death certificates are in Spanish and do not state the cause of death, which matters for destinations (such as the US) that require it unless the body is embalmed.

Post-mortem for all foreign nationals at the Pathology Institute

name: Puerto Rico
summary: Puerto Rico is a US territory, so a casket arriving from abroad is subject to the same federal CDC rules as the US mainland (42 CFR 71 expressly covers Puerto Rico): the remains must be in a leak-proof container and, unless embalmed, travel with a death certificate stating the cause of death. A licensed local funeral home receives the remains after CBP clearance.
documents: Death certificate stating the cause of death (English or with a translation), unless the remains are embalmed
Embalming certificate where the body is embalmed
Consular Report of Death Abroad or Consular Mortuary Certificate from the US embassy if the deceased was a US citizen
Removal or export permit from the country of departure
Passport of the deceased and air waybill or flight manifest
Name and contact of the receiving licensed funeral home in Puerto Rico
coffin: CDC requires all non-cremated remains to be fully contained in a leak-proof container (for example a casket with a leak-proof lining or a sealed metal transfer case). No territorial rule on zinc lining or witnessed sealing was found; the country of departure may impose a hermetically sealed zinc-lined coffin.
embalming: Not required by US federal rules for entry, but embalmed remains are exempt from the CDC death-certificate requirement. Remains of a person who died of certain infectious diseases may need a CDC import permit unless embalmed. Most departure countries and airlines require embalming anyway.
consular: No legalisation is required for entry. If a US citizen dies abroad, the US embassy or consulate can issue a Consular Report of Death Abroad and, where no death certificate exists, a Consular Mortuary Certificate. Foreign-language documents need an English translation.
arrival: CBP clears the remains at the first US port of entry, with CDC requirements checked against the documents. Under 42 CFR 71.55 the remains must go directly to a licensed mortuary, cemetery or crematory. Under Puerto Rico's Funeral Services Act (Law 258-2012), only registered funeral homes and funeral directors may receive a body into Puerto Rico, and the transfer and burial or cremation permit of a person who died outside Puerto Rico serves as proof of death.
private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; the documents travel with the coffin and are presented to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. The coffin (typically about 2.2 m long, 70-100 kg once zinc-lined) must physically fit the aircraft's cargo door or a cabin configured for it, which rules out many light and midsize jets. An international arrival into Puerto Rico must clear US Customs and Border Protection, so plan the flight to an airport where CBP clearance can be arranged in advance and have the receiving funeral home meet the aircraft. A flight from the US mainland is a domestic flight and needs no CBP entry, but the state burial-transit permit must travel with the remains.
private_jet_note: International arrivals must clear CBP; arrange clearance before take-off.
export: Under Law 258-2012, a transfer permit (permiso de traslado) is required only when the body leaves Puerto Rico; it is requested by the licensed funeral director from the Demographic Registry (Registro Demografico) or Environmental Health (Salud Ambiental) of the Department of Health, and the body cannot leave before it is issued. Airlines and shipping companies must ask for this permit and for the documents required by the destination. Every body leaving Puerto Rico must be embalmed by a licensed embalmer, except for the US: embalming is not required there if the death certificate shows no contagious or quarantinable disease and the body is in a leak-proof container. For destinations outside the US, the funeral director must contact the destination country's consulate and meet its requirements. Bodies under the Institute of Forensic Sciences cannot be embalmed without its authorisation.
export_points: Funeral director obtains the transfer permit from the Demographic Registry or Environmental Health
Embalming by a licensed embalmer required, except leak-proof transfers to the US
Destination consulate's requirements apply for international transfers
Forensic cases need Institute of Forensic Sciences approval before embalming

name: Saint Martin (France)
summary: Saint Martin (France) is a French overseas collectivity, so French rules apply: entry of a body from abroad is authorised by the French embassy or consulate in the country of departure, and an airtight (metal-lined) coffin is mandatory for air transport.
documents: Death certificate from the country of death (transcription into French civil status by the consulate is possible)

Embalming or conservation certificate where required by the departure country

coffin: For air transport an airtight coffin (metal box, in practice a soldered zinc lining inside a wooden coffin) is mandatory under French rules. A hermetically sealed coffin generally cannot be cremated without reopening, which is restricted.
embalming: France does not impose a single rule for incoming bodies; embalming or conservation care is normally required by the departure country and by carriers. Confirm with the consulate.
consular: The French embassy or consulate in the country of death authorises entry of the body into French territory and can transcribe the foreign death certificate. From Strasbourg Agreement states, the laissez-passer issued there is used. Families bear all costs.
arrival: The receiving funeral home takes charge at the airport. The French 14-day burial or cremation deadline counts from the body's entry into France; how it applies in the overseas collectivity was not confirmed, so check with the funeral home. Transfers between the collectivity and mainland France are authorised by the State's representative in the collectivity (towards mainland France) or by the prefect (from mainland France).
private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; the documents travel with the coffin and are presented to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. The coffin (typically about 2.2 m long, 70-100 kg once zinc-lined) must physically fit the aircraft's cargo door or a cabin configured for it, which rules out many light and midsize jets.  Saint Martin shares its island with Sint Maarten; Grand Case airport is small, so many coffin flights use Princess Juliana airport on the Dutch side. Confirm customs and transfer arrangements across the island in advance. The French airtight coffin rule applies to any air transport, including private flights.
private_jet_note: Airtight zinc-lined coffin mandatory for any flight.
export: To send a body out of French territory, the funeral home obtains authorisation from the State's representative (prefect) for the place where the coffin is closed; for this collectivity that is the prefect delegate for Saint-Barthelemy and Saint-Martin (confirm locally). An airtight coffin is mandatory for air transport, and the destination country's consular requirements also apply.

coffin: Not published officially. A hermetically sealed (usually zinc-lined) coffin in a wooden outer case is the usual standard for air transport; confirm with the local funeral home and the carrier.
embalming: No published entry rule. Embalming is normally required by the departure country and carriers; an embalming certificate is part of the export file.
consular: Not published officially. Ask the receiving funeral home whether foreign documents must be legalised or apostilled.
arrival: Not published officially. The receiving funeral home normally arranges customs and health clearance. There are no cremation facilities in Antigua or Barbuda; cremation is arranged abroad (for example Puerto Rico, Barbados or Grenada).
private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; the documents travel with the coffin and are presented to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. The coffin (typically about 2.2 m long, 70-100 kg once zinc-lined) must physically fit the aircraft's cargo door or a cabin configured for it, which rules out many light and midsize jets. Land at V. C. Bird International Airport with customs clearance arranged and have the receiving funeral home meet the aircraft. No specific rule for private flights carrying remains was found.
private_jet_note: Confirm entry documents with the local funeral home before take-off.
export: The death is registered with the Civil Registry, usually by the next of kin or a funeral director with a letter of authorisation; the certificate is issued in English within a few days and states the cause of death. Post-mortems are carried out by forensic doctors appointed by the hospital or court and their timing depends on the police investigation, which can delay release of the body. Local funeral directors provide the death certificate, a certificate of embalming and a certificate giving permission to transfer the remains. Infectious conditions must be reported to the local authorities.
export_points: Civil Registry death certificate in English, within a few days
Embalming certificate and permission to transfer required
Police-led post-mortem timing can delay release
No crematorium; cremation is arranged abroad

steps.what: Appoint a funeral home in Antigua and Barbuda and ask it to confirm entry requirements
Obtain death certificate, embalming certificate and removal permit in the country of death
Seal the coffin and send the documents ahead to the receiving funeral home
Fly to V. C. Bird International Airport with customs clearance arranged
Funeral home clears the coffin and arranges the burial

No cremation facilities in the country
Death certificates are in English and show the cause of death
